brief.summary: A rules-as-code authoring tool for academic law-and-computation labs that turn public-benefits eligibility law into executable decision logic, with every step tied to its statutory citation.
brief.user: Kwame Asante, a third-year PhD student in a university policy-informatics lab. He is encoding one state's SNAP eligibility rules for a study on how often caseworker determinations diverge from the law. He's fluent in both legal citation and logic.
brief.moment: He's building the income-test portion of the rule model. This morning he found that a 2025 state amendment changed how the gross-income test applies to households with an elderly or disabled member. His current logic treats them the same as everyone else, which is why 3 of his 12 test households fail. He needs to insert a new condition for elderly/disabled members, rewire the gross-income and net-income checks around it, attach the amended citation to each affected step, and rerun the test households until all pass.
brief.data: The rule model has 63 nodes (conditions, calculations and outcomes) with 81 connections between them. Each node cites a code section, such as 7 CFR 273.9(a) or state administrative rule 461-160-0015 (amended 2025). Income thresholds are stored as parameters by household size (1–8+): 130% FPL gross and 100% FPL net, effective Oct 1, 2026. There are 12 test households with expected outcomes written by the lab's legal advisor; 9 pass and 3 fail (cases T-04, T-07 and T-11, each with an elderly or disabled member). The version history has 27 saved revisions, and a lab-mate, Hye-jin, left 2 open notes on the deductions section.

prompt:
I need the front end for Statute Loom. A rules-as-code authoring tool for academic law-and-computation labs that turn public-benefits eligibility law into executable decision logic, with every step tied to its statutory citation.

Who's using it: Kwame Asante, a third-year PhD student in a university policy-informatics lab. He is encoding one state's SNAP eligibility rules for a study on how often caseworker determinations diverge from the law. He's fluent in both legal citation and logic.

What they're doing right now: He's building the income-test portion of the rule model. This morning he found that a 2025 state amendment changed how the gross-income test applies to households with an elderly or disabled member. His current logic treats them the same as everyone else, which is why 3 of his 12 test households fail. He needs to insert a new condition for elderly/disabled members, rewire the gross-income and net-income checks around it, attach the amended citation to each affected step, and rerun the test households until all pass.

What's in the system at this point: The rule model has 63 nodes (conditions, calculations and outcomes) with 81 connections between them. Each node cites a code section, such as 7 CFR 273.9(a) or state administrative rule 461-160-0015 (amended 2025). Income thresholds are stored as parameters by household size (1–8+): 130% FPL gross and 100% FPL net, effective Oct 1, 2026. There are 12 test households with expected outcomes written by the lab's legal advisor; 9 pass and 3 fail (cases T-04, T-07 and T-11, each with an elderly or disabled member). The version history has 27 saved revisions, and a lab-mate, Hye-jin, left 2 open notes on the deductions section.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
